name: cudaFoam (cudaPCG: GPU PCG pressure-solver plugin for OpenFOAM)
baseline: OpenFOAM 12 CPU GAMG and CPU PCG-DIC (single rank)
workload: OpenFOAM 12 incompressibleFluid pitzDaily tutorial scaled to 12,225 / 305,625 / 1,222,500 cells (1000 / 5 / 5 time steps); wall time of foamRun with the pressure equation solved by cudaPCG (cuSPARSE SpMV plus multicolor symmetric Gauss-Seidel preconditioner with FP32 sweeps) versus stock CPU GAMG and CPU PCG-DIC at identical tolerances.
claimed_speedup: vs CPU GAMG: 17.2 s -> 13.3 s (1.3x) at 305,625 cells and 95.0 s -> 88.3 s (1.08x) at 1,222,500 cells. vs CPU PCG-DIC: 56.0 s -> 13.3 s at 305,625 cells, 498 s -> 88.3 s (5.6x) at 1,222,500 cells, and 93.1 s -> 65.1 s at 12,225 cells (1000 steps; no GAMG run at that size).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc via Allwmake, default ARCH=sm_86, CUDA 12.x/13.x; OpenFOAM 12 build 12-86e126a7bc4d (from log header); optimization flags of the OpenFOAM CPU baseline are not stated
hardware: AWS g5.xlarge (NVIDIA A10G GPU), single CPU rank (nProcs 1); CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Symmetric matrices only (pressure/Laplacian-type equations); single rank and single GPU, otherwise it falls back to OpenFOAM's own PCG; requires an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA and OpenFOAM 12 (ESI v2412 compile-verified); GPL-3.0 because it builds against OpenFOAM; FP32 preconditioner sweeps with FP64 CG; GPU PCG needs far more iterations than GAMG.
caveats: Brand-new first-party repo with a single author; numbers are whole-case foamRun ExecutionTime (include non-pressure equations), not pressure-solve-only times. Margin over GAMG is small (1.08x at 1.2M cells); the large ratio is against CPU PCG-DIC, which is the weaker algorithm. Raw logs are in benchmark/results/: the tails of v4_huge_gpu.log (88.0046 s) and v4_huge_gamg.log (94.6959 s) differ slightly from the README's 88.3 s and 95.0 s. Pressure fields differ from the CPU reference by 0.017-0.06 percent of range on small/medium meshes and 0.56 percent at 1.2M cells (README says this is within GAMG-vs-PCG scatter). Baseline is OpenFOAM's solver, not one of SuiteSparse/Eigen sparse/PETSc. Benchmark mesh dicts and logs are public; CPU model and CPU baseline compile flags are not stated.

name: CapelliniSpTRSV (thread-level synchronization-free GPU sparse triangular solve)
baseline: cuSPARSE SpTRSV (CUSPARSE_SOLVE_POLICY_NO_LEVEL / USE_LEVEL) and the SyncFree SpTRSV of bhSPARSE
workload: Sparse triangular solve (CSR input, no level-set preprocessing) on 245 matrices from the Florida (SuiteSparse) Sparse Matrix Collection, three GPU platforms.
claimed_speedup: 3.41 GFLOPS/s, which is 5.26x speedup over the state-of-the-art synchronization-free SpTRSV algorithm and 4.00x speedup over the SpTRSV in cuSPARSE.
hardware: NVIDIA GTX 1080 (Pascal, CUDA 8.0, Ubuntu 16.04.4), Tesla V100 (Volta, CUDA 9.0, Ubuntu 16.04.1), GeForce RTX 2080 Ti (Turing, CUDA 10.2, Ubuntu 18.04.4); OpenCL variant tested on Radeon Vega 11 APU with ROCm; host CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: GPU-only research code (CUDA and OpenCL); takes CSR, so no format conversion; one folder per algorithm (SyncFree_csc, cuSP, cuSP-layer, our2Part, ourWrtFst, mix); precision and GPU parameters are edited in common.h and the CUDA path in each Makefile, which hard-codes sm_61.
caveats: Numbers are the paper abstract as reproduced in the README (ICPP '20 per the README citation); the paper itself was not opened. The README does not say which GPU or aggregation the 5.26x/4.00x refer to. cuSPARSE baseline is the CUDA 8-10.2 era SpTRSV; newer cuSPARSE versions were not tested. Authors note the win is for matrices with many components per level and few nonzeros per row. Last commit 2021. Host CPU model not stated, so not tier A.

name: SparseX (CSX-format SpMV library with LLVM runtime code generation)
baseline: Intel MKL inspector-executor SpMV (and CSR SpMV)
workload: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on multicore CPUs; the Compressed Sparse eXtended (CSX) format stores dense substructures compactly to cut memory bandwidth and emits specialised kernels per matrix.
claimed_speedup: For HPC matrices, up to 19.5x over the MKL inspector-executor SpMV kernel (1.6x on average) (snippet only).
tradeoffs: Needs LLVM/Clang >= 4.0, Boost >= 1.48 (regex, serialization, system), numactl and gcc >= 4.8 (README); autotools build; format conversion and tuning step before the first multiply, so it pays off only for repeated SpMV (iterative solvers).
caveats: Numbers come from a WebSearch result snippet only; the paper/page itself was not opened (arxiv, ACM, IEEE and researchgate hosts are EGRESS_BLOCKED in this environment), so tier is capped at C. The snippet came from a WebSearch summary of SparseX-related papers and its attribution to the SparseX TOMS paper was not verified. A different snippet (a 2025 third-party paper on index/value compression for SpMV) says SparseX is mainly able to reliably speed up SpMV for large matrices, median speedup 13 percent and geometric mean 7.7 percent; the baseline of that figure was not visible. The repo README itself carries no benchmark numbers and cites the TOMS, TPDS, IPDPS'13 and PPoPP'11 papers. Last commit 2018, so MKL has had many releases since.

name: GLU (GPU-accelerated sparse LU solver for circuit simulation)
workload: Sparse LU factorization of circuit-simulation matrices from the University of Florida (SuiteSparse) collection, GPU versus CPU direct solvers.
claimed_speedup: GLU solver delivers 19.56x speedup over the KLU solver and 47.13x over the UMFPACK solver on typical circuit matrices (snippet only).
tradeoffs: Needs CUDA (nvcc); README says the solver runs in single-precision float32 on the GPU, with float64 inputs/outputs converted at the boundary; CSC input; Python bindings (pyglu) and scipy-style splu wrapper; aimed at low-fill circuit matrices.
caveats: Numbers come from a WebSearch result snippet only; the paper/page itself was not opened (arxiv, ACM, IEEE and researchgate hosts are EGRESS_BLOCKED in this environment), so tier is capped at C. The README cites J1 (TVLSI 2016, GLU) and J2 (GLU3.0, IEEE Design & Test); the 19.56x / 47.13x figures appear to belong to the original GLU paper and it is unverified which code version, precision and timing scope (factorization only or full solve) they cover. A second snippet for GLU3.0 reports 13.0x (arithmetic mean) / 6.7x (geometric mean) over GLU2.0, which is not an external baseline. README itself has no benchmark numbers. Recent commits include bug fixes for a CUDA __syncthreads() deadlock and unchecked CUDA calls (README note, Feb 2026), so older published numbers were measured on code with those issues.

name: RA-SpMM (regime-aware GPU SpMM router for GNN workloads)
workload: Sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) with CSR sparse matrix and feature width N in {64,128,256,512} over 51 graphs (26 real, 25 synthetic) = 192 configurations on an RTX 3090; a seven-rule decision tree dispatches each call to one of five CSR or tensor-core tile kernels; warm protocol is 50 warmup + 200 timed CUDA-event iterations on both sides.
claimed_speedup: 1.702x warm geomean speedup over FP32 cuSPARSE (oracle 1.706x, 173/192 oracle hits); precision-matched speedup 1.222x; cold first-call 2.269x; GNN training step vs cuSPARSE backend 1.37x/1.26x/1.26x warm geomean (GCN/SAGE/GIN), up to 3.24x on Reddit; RTX 4090 transfer 1.515x warm.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 with -arch=sm_86 (setup.py, RA_SM_ARCH env var), CUDA 11.8 and matching PyTorch; CUDA 12.1 for the RTX 4090 sweep
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (primary) and RTX 4090 (cross-architecture); host CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: CUDA GPU only with PyTorch bindings; tile kernels need a one-time format build (1 ms to 36 ms geomean, worst 1.5 s per RESULTS.md) and tensor-core FP16/TF32 paths, so results are not bit-identical to FP32 cuSPARSE; a cuSPARSE guardrail covers inputs no specialist improves.
caveats: Paper is under review at Future Generation Computer Systems (README), so not peer reviewed yet: tier C although code, flags, per-table CSVs (CC-BY-4.0) and a reproduce script are public; host CPU model is missing. The headline 1.702x compares FP16/TF32 tensor-core kernels against FP32 cuSPARSE; precision-matched speedup is 1.222x (RESULTS.md: 1.053x on the RTX 4090). RESULTS.md also reports frozen-router validation on 9 unseen graphs at only 1.197x, FlashSparse being faster than the RA-SpMM router (1.28x geomean over 190 configs; FlashSparse faster on 134, router on 56), and a worst-case router/oracle ratio of 0.868x. Self-selected benchmark suite of GNN-style graphs; baseline cuSPARSE is not one of SuiteSparse/Eigen sparse/PETSc.
